Create, modify and delete columns

Source: R/mutate.R
mutate.tbl_gpu.Rd

mutate() adds new columns or changes existing ones, as dplyr::mutate() does. The expressions listed under "Supported expressions" are computed on the GPU, within the limits stated there. A call with any other expression runs in dplyr on the CPU, and its result comes back to the GPU.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
mutate(
  .data,
  ...,
  .by = NULL,
  .keep = c("all", "used", "unused", "none"),
  .before = NULL,
  .after = NULL
)

Arguments

.data

A tbl_gpu object created by tbl_gpu().

...

Name-value pairs of expressions. The name gives the column name (new or existing), and the value is an expression involving existing columns and/or scalar values (see "Supported expressions" below).

.by

Optional grouping columns for this call only (tidyselect), run on the GPU: mutate(df, y = mean(x), .by = g) gives the same result as df |> group_by(g) |> mutate(y = mean(x)) |> ungroup(), with the rows in their original order. The result is always ungrouped. Supplying .by when .data is already grouped (via group_by()) is an error, as in dplyr.

.keep

One of "all" (default), "used", "unused", "none"; controls which of .data's other columns (besides ones ... creates or modifies, and group columns, both of which are always kept) survive in the output – see ".keep semantics" below.

.before, .after

Optionally, control where new columns should appear, using the same tidyselect syntax as relocate.tbl_gpu(). Only new columns are moved; a modified existing column stays where it is.

Value

A tbl_gpu object with the new or modified columns. If a column name already exists, it is replaced. New columns are appended (subject to .before/.after), and .data's other columns are kept or dropped per .keep.

Details

.keep semantics

As in dplyr, the columns created or modified by ... (every dot's output column, new or replaced) and every grouping column are always kept, whatever .keep says. .keep only controls which other (untouched, non-grouping) columns of .data are kept alongside them:

  • "all" (default): every other column.

  • "used": other columns that are referenced as an input to any of ...'s expressions (union across all dots).

  • "unused": other columns not referenced as an input to any expression – the complement of "used".

  • "none": no other columns at all.

Column order: .data's columns keep their order (modified columns don't move), and new columns are appended at the end (or placed with .before/.after); .keep then drops columns without changing that order. This differs from transmute(), whose output order is the literal ... dot order (see transmute()'s own docs).

Supported expressions

A function runs on the GPU only when its name, in the expression's environment, is the base, dplyr or lubridate function itself: a function of your own with the same name (local, in an enclosing function or global) runs on the CPU, as dplyr would call it, and pkg::fn is the function of that package. The same holds for a function passed as a value (across(x, f), a list of functions held in a variable, !!f) and for the functions and lambdas of the scoped verbs (mutate_at(), summarise_all(), filter_if(), ...): one that is, or calls, a function of yours with the name of a GPU function runs on the CPU. These run on the GPU:

  • Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, ^, %%, %/%, unary -, nested to any depth ((x + y) * z - 1), with a scalar on either side (mutate(y = 10 - x))

  • Comparisons and logic: ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=, &, |, !, xor() – these produce a logical column, e.g. mutate(is_big = x > 100). Two strings compare with ==, !=, %in% and between() on the GPU whatever the session's collation. <, <=, > and >= of strings compare bytes on the GPU, while R uses the session's collation, so they run on the GPU only when Sys.getlocale("LC_COLLATE") is "C" or "POSIX", and in dplyr on the CPU otherwise. A string compared with a number runs on the CPU (R compares them as strings).

  • is.na(), is.nan(), between(x, lo, hi), near(x, y, tol = ) (abs(x - y) < tol, as dplyr::near() defines it), %in% (including a bare NA on the right-hand side, e.g. x %in% NA, as NA %in% NA is TRUE in base R; an empty set is always FALSE)

  • Math functions: sqrt(), log() (including log(x, base)), log2(), log10(), exp(), abs(), floor(), ceiling(), sin(), cos(), tan(), round(x)/round(x, digits) (banker's rounding, as in R)

  • String functions, among them nchar(), toupper(), tolower(), substr(), trimws(), startsWith(), endsWith(); paste() and paste0() when every argument is a string (a number or a logical argument runs on the CPU), with a constant sep and no collapse; and grepl(), sub() and gsub() with a constant pattern (ignore.case, perl and useBytes run on the CPU)

  • Dates and date-times: a Date plus or minus a whole number of days, lubridate's year(), month(), day(), hour(), minute(), second(), quarter(), yday(), wday(), floor_date(), ceiling_date() and round_date(), and as.Date()/as.POSIXct(), for the arguments the GPU supports; other forms run on the CPU

  • A factor column compared with a label (f == "a", f %in% c("a", "b"), and <, >, ... for an ordered factor), and as.character(), as.integer() or as.numeric() of a factor column

  • if_else(cond, yes, no, missing = NULL) – strict-but-promoting type unification across yes/no/missing (int/double/logical mix freely, like dplyr's vctrs-based common type; STRING only unifies with STRING). An NA condition produces NA (or missing, if supplied) in the output, as in dplyr (this is not the same as treating an NA condition like FALSE)

  • case_when(cond1 ~ val1, cond2 ~ val2, ..., .default = val) – first-match-wins; an NA condition is treated as no match (falls through to the next clause, or .default); unmatched rows become a typed NA when .default isn't supplied; the same value-type unification rule as if_else() applies across every val_i plus .default. A call with .ptype=, .size= or .unmatched= runs on the CPU.

  • coalesce(...) – first non-NA value per row, left to right, across any number of columns/scalars; same value-type unification rule as if_else()

  • na_if(x, y) – x with NA wherever x == y; the output always keeps x's own type (unlike if_else()/coalesce(), y is never promoted into the result, only compared against)

  • case_match(.x, old_values ~ new_value, ..., .default = val) – matches .x by value against each clause's (possibly multi-element) left-hand side, first match wins; NA on a clause's left-hand side matches .x's own NA elements (base R's NA %in% NA is TRUE); unmatched rows become .default (typed NA if not supplied), with the same value-type unification rule as case_when() across every new_value plus .default. dplyr 1.2 deprecates it in favor of recode_values()/replace_values(); it still runs on the GPU. A call with .ptype= runs on the CPU.

  • recode(.x, old = new, ..., .default =, .missing =) – on the GPU only for a bare character/integer/double column .x and scalar literal replacements of one shared type (dplyr::recode, including !!! lookups); duplicate keys, factor .x, recode_factor(), and a result type different from .x without .default run on the CPU.

  • recode_values(x, old_values ~ new_value, ..., default = val) – the non-deprecated equivalent of case_match() above (the same semantics, default instead of .default). The from=/to= lookup-table form and unmatched=/ptype= run on the CPU.

  • replace_values(x, old_values ~ new_value, ...) – like recode_values(), but type stable: the output always keeps x's own type (every new_value is cast to it, never unified/promoted), and unmatched rows keep their original x value (there is no default=). The from=/to= form runs on the CPU.

  • replace_when(x, cond1 ~ val1, cond2 ~ val2, ...) – like case_when(), but with the type-stable, "unmatched rows keep x" behavior of replace_values() (an NA condition is treated as no match, as in case_when())

  • when_all(..., na_rm = FALSE) / when_any(..., na_rm = FALSE) – elementwise &/| generalized to any number of logical inputs (when_any(x, y, z) is x | y | z). na_rm = TRUE treats NA as each operator's identity element (FALSE for when_any(), TRUE for when_all()) rather than propagating it – e.g. when_any(NA, NA, na_rm = TRUE) is FALSE, not NA. A call with size= runs on the CPU.

  • Plain column copies (mutate(y = x))

  • A later dot in the same mutate() call referencing an earlier dot's output column (mutate(a = x + y, b = a * 2)), also when it is a window function's output (mutate(a = cumsum(x), b = lag(a)))

  • The .data/.env pronouns, and ordinary R symbols (a bare name that matches a column resolves to that column; otherwise it is looked up as an R variable: columns shadow the environment, as in dplyr)

  • Window functions, on ungrouped and grouped (group_by()) tables, nested to any depth with any of the above (mutate(y = x - lag(x)), mutate(z = lag(cumsum(x))), mutate(centered = x - mean(x))):

    • row_number() (sequential position) / row_number(x) (ranked position, ties broken by original position) – per-group under group_by()

    • lag(x, n = 1, default = NA, order_by = NULL) / lead(...) – a shift that keeps the row order; order_by= (a bare column, desc(column), or -column) makes the shift follow that ordering instead of the table's/group's current row order

    • cumsum()/cummax()/cummin()/cumprod() – with R's NA propagation (cumsum(c(1, 2, NA, 4)) is 1, 3, NA, NA: once an NA is seen, every later cumulative value in that group is NA too). The cumsum() of an integer or logical is an integer that is NA from the first overflow on (with R's warning), as in R

    • cummean() (cumsum(x) / row_number(), accumulated in double), cumall()/cumany(), and consecutive_id() of one column (a group id that increases whenever the value changes; adjacent NAs count as unchanged)

    • min_rank()/dense_rank()/percent_rank()/cume_dist() – ties and NA as in dplyr (NA input -> NA rank; percent_rank() is (min_rank(x) - 1) / (n_non_NA - 1), NaN for a group with exactly one non-NA value, as dplyr's NaN, not NA; cume_dist() is rank(x, ties = "max") / n_non_NA)

    • roll_mean(), roll_sum(), roll_min(), roll_max() and roll_sd(), and data.table's frollmean(), frollsum(), frollmin(), frollmax() and frollsd() with their default align, fill, adaptive, partial and give.names; roll_median() runs on the CPU. roll_min()/roll_max() of an integer, logical, Date or POSIXct column keep its type, where dplyr returns a double

    • mean()/sum()/min()/max()/n()/sd()/var()/ median()/n_distinct() – one aggregate broadcast to every row of its group (or the whole table, ungrouped); mean()/sum()/min()/max()/sd()/var()/median() follow R's na.rm = FALSE default (any NA in the group makes that group's result NA); n() always counts every row regardless of NAs, and n_distinct() counts NA as a value. median() runs on the GPU for a double, Date or POSIXct column (of an integer or logical one, on the CPU), and min()/max() of a string column under the collation rule of the comparisons above. On the GPU, mean() and median() of a Date are floored to whole days with a cuplyr_warning_fractional_date warning, where dplyr keeps the fractional Date. sum() of an integer or logical is an integer, as in dplyr. When a sum leaves the integer range dplyr returns a double (for the whole column, and for any expression on it): the call is then rerun by dplyr on the CPU. A lazy table can't plan for that (the type depends on the data), so a lazy mutate() with an integer sum() runs at the verb like an eager one (a plan break first runs the pending steps) and returns a lazy table with nothing pending; a logical sum() stays in the plan (it overflows only past 2^31 TRUE rows, with a cuplyr_error_sum_overflow at collect())

    • first(x, order_by = NULL) / last(x, order_by = NULL) / nth(x, n, order_by = NULL) – the first/last/nth row of the group in its current row order, or in order_by's order when supplied; negative n counts from the end (nth(x, -1) == last(x)); an out-of-range n gives NA. A call with default= or na_rm= runs on the CPU.

    • ntile(x = row_number(), n)

    • order_by(order_by, call) / with_order(order_by, fun, x, ...) – as in dplyr, only the first argument of call is put in order_by's order (stable, NA last); the other arguments are evaluated in row order, and the call stays on the GPU only when each of them is a non-NULL scalar that reads no column. On the GPU: a window call wrapped directly (cumsum()/cummax()/cummin()/ cumprod()/lag()/lead()/roll_*() except roll_median(), and cummean()/cumall()/cumany()/consecutive_id()), the rank functions that depend only on the values (min_rank(), dense_rank(), ... are unaffected by the order), and an elementwise call whose other arguments are scalars (order_by(o, cumsum(x) * 2) is cumsum(x) * 2: the window inside the first argument runs in row order, as in dplyr). Everything else runs the whole call on the CPU, which gives dplyr's value or error: roll_median(), an elementwise call with another column argument (order_by(o, cumsum(x) + lag(x))), a NULL or empty extra argument (lag(x, default = NULL)), row_number(x)/ntile(x, n) (ties broken by the order), first()/last()/nth(), aggregates, a nested order_by() as the wrapped call itself (order_by(o, order_by(i, cumsum(x))); nested inside the first argument it stays on the GPU), and shapes dplyr rejects (order_by(o, row_number()))

    Every one of these is evaluated within each group_by() group when .data is grouped, as in dplyr: the rows keep their order in the output (unlike grouped slice()).

Column replacement behavior

When the output column name matches an existing column, the existing column is replaced in-place (preserving column order). For example, mutate(x = x + 1) will modify x rather than creating a duplicate.

Result type (type promotion)

The output column's type follows from the operation and its inputs (the column types and, for a column-scalar expression, the R literal's own type), as in R:

  • A plain column copy (mutate(y = x)) preserves the source column's type exactly.

  • Arithmetic on a string column is an error, as in R. Arithmetic on a factor column runs in dplyr on the CPU (dplyr warns and gives NA). A Date plus or minus a whole number of days stays on the GPU; other date and date-time arithmetic (t + 3600 on a POSIXct, the difference of two dates, ...) runs in dplyr on the CPU.

  • / and ^ always give a double, as in R (1L / 2L and 2L ^ 2L are both doubles).

  • +, -, *, %%, %/% keep integers: the result is an integer when every input column and R literal involved is integer or logical (TRUE + TRUE is 2L, as in R). Like R, an integer +, - or * whose result leaves .Machine$integer.max is NA with the warning "NAs produced by integer overflow" (once per call; at collect() for a lazy table), and %/%/%% by 0L are NA. If any input is a double, the result is a double; otherwise, if any input is an integer64, the result is an integer64. A bare R numeric literal (e.g. the 1 in mutate(y = int_col + 1)) is a double in R, so it makes the result a double – write 1L to keep an integer result.

  • Comparisons, logic, is.na(), between(), %in% all produce a logical column.

  • sqrt(), log(), exp(), floor(), ceiling(), sin(), cos(), tan() always give a double, as in R (floor(1L) is a double), and so does round() (typeof(round(1L)) is also a double in R, unlike abs() below).

  • abs() preserves the argument's type, except a logical column, which becomes an integer (as in R: typeof(abs(TRUE)) is "integer", not "logical").

  • A bare NA (untyped) is logical when it is an entire mutate expression by itself (mutate(y = NA), as typeof(NA)); as an operand inside an arithmetic expression (mutate(y = int_col + NA)) it takes the other operand's type (as in R: 1L + NA is an integer, not a double). A typed NA literal (NA_real_, NA_integer_, ...) always keeps its own type.

Runs on the CPU

An expression that is not in the list above, or that uses a form the list sends to the CPU, runs the whole mutate() call in dplyr on the CPU (set options(cuplyr.fallback = "warn") to be told when; see cuplyr-fallback). So does an argument type for which the GPU would not give R's result, for example cummax() of a logical column, or sum(), mean(), min() or max() of an integer64 column. Among the other cases:

  • order_by()/with_order() with a general expression as the ordering argument (only a bare column, desc(column), or -column is on the GPU, with - for numeric/logical columns and desc() of a string only under a C collation: order_by(a + b, cumsum(x)) runs on the CPU); see the order_by() item above for what the wrapped call may be on the GPU

  • consecutive_id(a, b, ...) of more than one column

  • Sliding-window functions other than the roll_*() family (slider::slide_*() and similar)

  • The arguments named in the items above: case_when()'s and case_match()'s .ptype=/.size=/.unmatched=, recode_values()'s and replace_values()'s from=/to= and unmatched=/ptype=, and when_all()'s and when_any()'s size=

Performance

GPU arithmetic is highly parallel; memory bandwidth is usually the limiting factor, not compute.

See also

filter.tbl_gpu for filtering rows, select.tbl_gpu for selecting columns, collect.tbl_gpu for retrieving results

Examples

library(dplyr)
if (has_gpu()) {
  gpu_mtcars <- tbl_gpu(mtcars)

  # Add a new column
  result <- gpu_mtcars |>
    mutate(kpl = mpg * 0.425) |>
    collect()

  # Modify an existing column
  adjusted <- gpu_mtcars |>
    mutate(mpg = mpg + 5) |>
    collect()

  # Combine two columns
  gpu_cars <- tbl_gpu(cars)
  result <- gpu_cars |>
    mutate(ratio = dist / speed) |>
    collect()

  # Chain multiple mutations
  result <- gpu_mtcars |>
    mutate(power_weight = hp / wt) |>
    mutate(efficiency = mpg * power_weight) |>
    collect()
}
